course.title: AP United States History
course.description: A vertical-video APUSH course organized as units, chapters, lessons, and instructional scenes.
course.audience: APUSH students preparing for class assessments and the AP exam

presentation.visual_style: museum-documentary visuals with readable AP exam vocabulary

units.title: Period 1: Worlds Before and After Contact
units.description: Indigenous societies before European arrival, Atlantic exploration, the Columbian Exchange, and the first Spanish systems of conquest and labor.
learning_objectives: Explain how geography shaped diverse Indigenous societies before European contact.
Explain the causes and effects of European exploration in the Americas.
Evaluate how the Columbian Exchange transformed societies on both sides of the Atlantic.

chapters.title: Conquest and the Columbian Exchange
chapters.description: How Spain toppled the Mexica and Inca empires, how silver and forced labor built a colonial economy, and how the Columbian Exchange transformed both hemispheres.
essential_questions: How did a few hundred Spaniards topple empires of millions?
Why did the Columbian Exchange enrich some societies while devastating others?
learning_objectives: Explain how disease, Native alliances, and technology combined to enable Spanish conquest.
Trace the two-way biological and commercial flows of the Columbian Exchange.
Evaluate how silver mining and forced labor connected the Americas to a global economy.

lessons.title: How 500 Men Toppled an Empire
lessons.description: The paradox of Spanish conquest: how disease, Native alliances, and technology — not guns alone — toppled the Mexica and Inca empires.
lessons.essential_question: How did a few hundred Spaniards topple empires of millions?
learning_objectives: Explain why guns alone cannot account for Spanish victories.
Identify the roles of smallpox, the Tlaxcalans, and steel and horses in the conquests.
Compare the falls of Tenochtitlan (1521) and the Inca state (1532-33) as one pattern.

key_terms.definition: Spanish conquerors who toppled the Mexica and Inca empires in the 1500s.
An Afro-Eurasian disease that devastated Indigenous populations lacking immunity.
Enemies of the Mexica who allied with Cortés, supplying tens of thousands of warriors.

narration.text: Cusco was the capital of an empire that ruled millions, stretching from the Andes to the sea. [beat] In 1533 [emphasis]a few hundred Spaniards[/emphasis] seized it. Just as [es]Cortés[/es] had toppled the [es]Mexica[/es] empire a decade earlier. Guns alone cannot explain this. [urgent] So how did a few hundred men conquer worlds of millions?

animation.prompt: A de Bry engraving of the Inca capital Cusco. Clouds drift slowly over the mountain ridges; wind stirs the trees along the rocky slopes; thin haze moves through the distant valley; dust drifts softly over the empty rooftops. Keep the camera static. Do not add people or text or modern objects.
animation.caption: Cusco: an empire of millions, taken by a few hundred

beats.text: How did a few hundred conquer millions?

scenes.production_notes: Open on the scale of the city, then slam the paradox question over it.

narration.text: Smallpox traveled ahead of the armies and [emphasis]killed far more people[/emphasis] than any battle. The [es]Tlaxcalans[/es], enemies of the [es]Mexica[/es], sent tens of thousands of warriors to fight beside [es]Cortés[/es]. Horses and steel gave the Spanish an edge in close combat. [beat] Victory was a system: [fast]disease, alliances, and technology working together[/fast].

bullets: Disease first: smallpox killed more than any battle
Alliances: the Tlaxcalans sent tens of thousands of warriors
Edges, not miracles: steel swords and horses in close combat
Victory was a system — disease, alliances, technology

animation.caption: Mechanism, Not Myth

narration.text: [es]Cortés[/es] reached [es]Tenochtitlan[/es] in 1519 and found an empire strained by tribute and rivalries he learned to exploit. [beat] After smallpox ravaged the city, his coalition took it in 1521. A decade later [es]Pizarro[/es] copied the formula in Peru: [emphasis]seize the emperor [es]Atahualpa[/es] in 1532[/emphasis], and the Inca state fractured. Two empires, one pattern.

events: Cortés lands in Mexico; learns Mexica rivalries
Smallpox ravages Tenochtitlan during the siege
Pizarro seizes Atahualpa; the Inca state fractures

narration.text: [slow]Conquest was not the end of the story. It was the foundation of everything that followed.[/slow] Spanish rule replaced tribute empires with colonial labor systems. The mines, the sugar plantations, and the flow of goods across the Atlantic all rested on what the [es]conquistadors[/es] had seized. [emphasis]To understand the exchange, start with the conquest.[/emphasis]

lessons.title: The Exchange, Both Ways
lessons.description: Contact connected ecosystems separated for thousands of years: crops, animals, and diseases flowed in both directions — with growth on one side and catastrophe on the other.
lessons.essential_question: Why did the same exchange produce growth and catastrophe at once?
learning_objectives: List the major crops, animals, and diseases that crossed the Atlantic in each direction.
Explain how American crops supported population growth in Afro-Eurasia.
Use causation and comparison to weigh the exchange's unequal effects.

key_terms.definition: The transfer of plants, animals, diseases, people, and ideas between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres after 1492.
Rapid population growth in Afro-Eurasia supported in part by calorie-rich American crops.
Outbreaks of Afro-Eurasian diseases that caused catastrophic Indigenous mortality in the Americas.

narration.text: For thousands of years, the Americas and Afro-Eurasia developed in isolation: [fast]separate crops, separate animals, separate diseases[/fast]. [beat] Columbus's voyages [emphasis]ended that isolation forever[/emphasis]. From 1492 on, plants, animals, pathogens, and people moved across the Atlantic in both directions, year after year. Historians call it the Columbian Exchange.

animation.prompt: A Stradanus engraving of a sugar refinery interior. Smoke and steam billow upward from the boiling cauldrons; flames flicker in the furnaces; cane leaves stir through the open arches; dust drifts in the shafts of daylight. Keep the camera static. Do not add people or text or modern objects.
animation.caption: Two worlds, one exchange

narration.text: Eastward sailed the American crops: [fast]maize, potatoes, tomatoes, and tobacco[/fast]. Potatoes and maize produced more calories per acre than most European grains, and they grew where wheat could not. [beat] Better-fed populations grew larger. By 1700, Europe and Africa held tens of millions more people than American foods had helped make possible.

bullets: Potatoes and maize: more calories per acre
They grew where European wheat could not

narration.text: Westward came wheat, sugarcane, horses, and pigs. [beat] And the deadliest cargo of all: [slow][solemn]smallpox, measles, and other Afro-Eurasian diseases[/slow]. Epidemics devastated Indigenous communities that had no immunity. [awed]The horse had the happiest outcome: it reached the Plains and turned mounted hunters into the continent's most mobile powers.

scenes.production_notes: The disease label should feel like a gut punch; the horse ending is the turn.

narration.text: The exchange [emphasis]gave with one hand and took with the other[/emphasis]. Afro-Eurasia gained crops that fed a population boom; the Americas gained livestock and new foods but lost up to nine-tenths of their people to disease. [beat] For the AP exam, compare both directions and [emphasis]weigh multiple causes[/emphasis]: the same ships carried growth and catastrophe.

lessons.title: Potosí: The Silver Mountain
lessons.description: Potosí's silver mines, the mita labor draft, and the price revolution — how one Andean mountain wired the first global economy.
lessons.essential_question: How did one mountain of silver wire the first global economy?
learning_objectives: Describe how the mita draft supplied labor for Potosí's silver mines.
Explain the price revolution as an effect of American silver in Europe.
Trace silver's path from Potosí to the Manila galleons and the global economy.

key_terms.definition: The Andean silver-mining center whose output bankrolled Spain's empire after 1545.
The Spanish colonial labor draft requiring Indigenous communities to send workers to the mines.
The century-long rise of European prices driven by the flood of American silver.

narration.text: [awed]High in the Andes sat a mountain so rich in silver that Spain built an empire on it. When miners struck the [es]Cerro Rico[/es] at [es]Potosí[/es] in 1545, they tapped one of the richest silver deposits in the world. [beat] For the next two centuries, this one mountain would [emphasis]bankroll Spain's wars[/emphasis], its bureaucracy, and its dreams of global power.

animation.prompt: A de Bry engraving of the Potosí silver mines. Clouds drift over the peak of the great mountain; wind stirs the lone tree on the ridge; smoke rises from the refining fires; dust moves along the mountain paths. Keep the camera static. Do not add people or text or modern objects.
animation.caption: 1545: a mountain of silver

source.title: Mitayos at the Potosí silver mine
source.creator: Theodor de Bry
source.notes: De Bry was a Dutch Protestant depicting Spanish cruelty — read the image as both evidence of labor and anti-Spanish argument.

scenes.production_notes: Hold on the mountain; let the scale of the claim register before the labor scene.

narration.text: The silver came at [emphasis]a human price[/emphasis]. Spain revived the Inca labor draft as the mita: Indigenous communities had to send a share of their men to the mines each year. [slow]Mitayos climbed down ladders into freezing tunnels, crushed ore by hand, and breathed mercury fumes.[/slow] [solemn]Many never came home. And the dying workforce pushed Spain toward enslaved African labor.

highlights.label: Mitayos climb the ladders carrying ore
Overseers with tools drive the work

narration.text: Silver crossed the Atlantic in [emphasis]staggering quantities[/emphasis], roughly forty-five thousand tons between 1500 and 1800. [beat] All that metal chased the same goods, and prices across Europe rose for a century: the price revolution. Spain spent the windfall on wars and imports instead of industry, so the silver [emphasis]enriched its rivals[/emphasis] more than itself.

narration.text: [es]Potosí[/es]'s silver did not stop in Spain. [beat] It flowed on to Asia, where China hungered for silver to run its tax system. Each year the Manila galleons carried American silver across the Pacific and returned with Chinese silks and porcelain. [awed]One mountain in the Andes had wired the [emphasis]first truly global economy[/emphasis].
